lines.text: Boeing just lost about sixteen billion dollars in a single day.
And the reason is sitting right outside your window seat.
Boeing, ticker [B-A](/bˈi ˈA/), fell almost eleven percent on Tuesday,
its worst day in more than a year and a half.
The strange part?
Its order book just hit a record seven hundred forty-five billion dollars. That's more than sixty-three hundred jets.
So what spooked investors?
The wait.
Boeing wanted to deliver around five hundred of its seven-thirty-seven jets this year. Nine months in, it has delivered three hundred sixty-seven, and it now says it won't get there.
Next year's free cash? Three billion dollars. Wall Street wanted five and a half.
But here's the twist almost no one is mentioning.
It isn't demand, and it isn't engines.
It's the wings. Boeing builds every seven-thirty-seven wing itself, and says that's still its biggest bottleneck.
Why does that matter?
Because airlines pay most of a jet's price on delivery.
An order is a promise. A delivery is cash.
And a steady forty-seven jets a month now slips to early twenty twenty-seven.
The market isn't asking if Boeing can sell planes.
It's asking if it can build the wings.
Buying chance, or warning sign? Tell me in the comments.
And follow for the daily market story.
